Quark. Quarks are fundamental fermions that carry color charge and are confined within hadrons via the strong nuclear force. Six flavors exist—up, down, charm, strange, bottom, top—spanning three generations. Quarks possess spin one-half and fractional electric charge, and their interaction via gluons forms the basis of quantum chromodynamics.

The six quark flavors are grouped into three generations. The up-type quarks carry an electric charge of plus two-thirds, while the down-type quarks carry minus one-third. All quarks are spin one-half fermions that obey the Pauli exclusion principle. They carry color charge—red, green, blue, and anticolors—which is required for strong force interaction. The lightest quarks, up and down, are the building blocks of ordinary matter. Antiquarks exist with opposite charge and color for each flavor.

Quarks represent the deepest level of matter structure accessible to experiment. Unlike leptons, quarks are permanently trapped inside composite particles through color confinement, a phenomenon unique to the strong force. The discovery of quarks unified seemingly diverse particles—baryons and mesons—under a single framework and explained strange particle decays through quark flavor mixing. Quarks cannot exist free; they remain confined within hadrons as partons. All hadrons are bound states of quarks, whether as three quarks in baryons or as quark-antiquark pairs in mesons, with gluons mediating the strong force between them.
